cards.title: Write ads as salesmanship in print
cards.summary: Claude Hopkins' core test: every ad, headline, and creative decision should be judged by whether it would help a live salesperson close the sale to one prospect standing in front of him.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing any acquisition creative — Meta/TikTok ad, product page hero, landing page, or email subject line — and you need a single test to cut indecision.
steps: Before finalizing a creative, ask: 'Would this help a salesman sell the goods if I met the buyer in person?' If the line only exists to be clever or short, cut it.
Do not shorten copy just because people 'read very little.' Hopkins's point: you would never hand a real prospect to a salesman and cap him at 10 words. Length is not the constraint — relevance is.

Because advertising 'may appeal to thousands while the salesman will talk to one,' a mediocre ad damages every prospect at once, whereas a mediocre salesman only wastes one conversation. Apply the higher bar to the ad.

Rewrite any line that would embarrass a salesperson saying it face-to-face — especially boasts, brand commands, and 'avoid imitations' style warnings, which Hopkins says indicate a motive buyers cannot sympathize with.
Check the final creative against one question: does every sentence increase good impression and speak to the prospect's desire, not the advertiser's pride?
caveats: This is Hopkins's framework from early-1900s direct-response advertising; the 'salesman' test is a reasoning tool, not a measured conversion benchmark.
Longer copy is not automatically better — the test is relevance and sales-helpfulness, not word count.

cards.title: Sell service, not your brand
cards.summary: Hopkins argues the two greatest faults in advertising are boasts and selfishness; replace 'buy my brand' appeals with a clearly unselfish offer of service to the customer.
cards.use_when: Drafting ad copy or landing page hero sections where the instinct is to lead with the brand name, product features, or company achievements.
steps: Identify every self-referential line in the creative — company history, plant size, awards, 'we're the best' claims — and tag each as a boast to be removed or reframed.
Rewrite each as the customer benefit that follows from it. The size of your plant, for example, becomes a reason the buyer gets faster shipping or lower risk.

Make the salesperson's plea match Hopkins's model: 'I was selling service... the advantage to myself was covered up in my efforts to please him.' The buyer should feel you are solving their problem, not asking a favor.

Apply the same to creative in competitive categories: Hopkins says you cannot enter a well-occupied field on a plain 'buy my brand' appeal, because it is repugnant. Offer exceptional service to induce switching from a favorite brand.

Re-audit existing top-of-funnel ads monthly. Hopkins's observation is that most advertisers merely 'cry a name' and their evident desire is selfish advantage — such advertising may pay somewhat but never as well as apparent unselfishness.
caveats: Hopkins presents this as a general principle ('argue for your own advantage and people will resist to the limit'), not a tested conversion lift.
Service framing still needs a real differentiator or specific promise; empty service language without substance is just another kind of vacancy.

cards.title: Advertise to one person, not the masses
cards.summary: Treat every inquirer as an individual prospect who walked into a store, with a specific need — not as a mass to be sent the same generic catalog or ad.
cards.use_when: Setting up email capture, retargeting sequences, PDP recommendations, or paid traffic flows where all visitors currently get the same generic response.
steps: Segment the entry point by expressed intent. Hopkins's example: a woman writing about a sewing machine should receive the sewing-machine catalog with every style and price, not the full company catalog sent to all inquiries alike.

Add social proof local to the prospect. Hopkins sent names of every buyer in the inquirer's town and asked her to go see the machine and talk to owners. For ecommerce, substitute nearby reviews, UGC, or a demo they can inspect in person.
Treat 'people in the mass' as a mistake. Hopkins: 'We must get down to individuals. We must treat people in advertising as we treat them in person.'
Apply this to retargeting and email: an ad creative that speaks to the searched category won't work for a cold, broad audience — match the creative to the individual's demonstrated desire.
Build the flow so a person who showed one specific intent gets one specific, complete answer (product, price, proof) rather than being routed to everything you sell.
caveats: Hopkins describes this principle from letter-inquiry handling, not digital funnels; the metaphor is the transferable part, not the mechanics.
Personalizing by intent requires enough traffic or data per segment; below that, use one clear offer rather than leaking budget across thin segments.

cards.title: Tell the pains you take (the Schlitz story)
cards.summary: Reveal the ordinary manufacturing and quality steps you take, even if competitors do the same, because nobody has told the story in print and it creates perceived distinction.
cards.use_when: Writing a product page, brand story section, or ad angle for a commodity-like product where you believe 'everyone does this, so it's not a differentiator.'
steps: Do first-hand research at the source of production — visit the facility, interview the operators, ask why every step exists. Hopkins saw plate-glass rooms, white wood-pulp filters, pipes cleaned twice daily, bottles cleaned four times by machinery, 4,000-ft artisan wells, six-month aging, and a mother yeast developed by 1,200 experiments.
Capture each step's purpose, not just its existence. For ecommerce, that could be inspection steps, material sourcing, QA thresholds, or fulfillment processes.

Resist the founder's reflex that it's just ordinary. Hopkins's clients said 'the processes we use are just the same as others' — his answer: 'Others have never told this story... It will startle everyone in print.'
Write the process into the PDP or ad as a purity/quality narrative with concrete numbers and specifics, giving your claim a visible meaning instead of merely repeating 'pure' or 'premium'.

Test this against your current PDP claims: 'the maker is too close to his product. He sees in his methods only the ordinary.' The steps you find boring are exactly what a buyer has never seen explained.
caveats: Schlitz allegedly went from fifth to neck-and-neck with first after the campaign — a case-study result attributed to the source, not a promised outcome.
The technique works only if the claimed process is true and verifiable; inventing hidden steps is not the method, and it can be easily exposed.

cards.title: Sell painkillers, not prevention
cards.summary: Prevention and disaster-avoidance are weak appeals; Hopkins found people will do anything to cure a trouble but little to prevent it, so advertise rewards, beauty, happiness, and desirable outcomes.
cards.use_when: Choosing the angle for health, wellness, supplement, dental, financial, or maintenance-focused products where the default pitch is risk prevention.
steps: Write both angles for the same product: the prevention angle ('use this so your teeth don't decay') and the reward angle ('use this to become more attractive, happier, more cheerful').

Hopkins's Pepso dent decision: he resolved to advertise the toothpaste as a creator of beauty rather than a preventative. Apply the same shift to skincare, supplements, supplements-for-prevention, or device warranties.
Never picture the afflicted in creative. Hopkins says he never referred to disasters and every illustration he used showed attractive people. Shoot and select creators accordingly.
Frame recurring-purchase products around the positive identity the customer attains, not the loss they avoid, because that is what drives the buying psychology.

Use the appeal audit across the whole campaign: Hopkins says every campaign depends on its psychology and success is determined by right or wrong appeal — so pick one dominant psychological appeal and make all ad variants consistent with it before testing.
caveats: Hopkins made a reported million dollars on Pepso dent from this psychological choice — a dramatic historical case, not a benchmark for modern conversion rates.
Reward positioning must still be honest and compliant; beauty/outcome claims in regulated categories (supplements, health) may need legal review.

cards.title: Sample the right way: require an effort
cards.summary: Free samples and demos work only when the user requests them or earns them; promiscuous sampling destroys perceived value, so gate samples behind an action.
cards.use_when: Designing lead magnets, free-trial offers, sample distribution, or PR-box mailers — deciding whether to send product free or require an opt-in.
steps: Do not propend samples on people who didn't ask. Hopkins: 'I have never found that it paid to give samples to people who do not request it... Products handed out without asking lose respect.'
Gate the sample behind a small action — filling out a request form, giving an email, completing a quiz. 'It is different when you force people to make an effort.'
Sequence it: 'We must arouse interest in our product before it has value to anybody.' Use the ad or PDP to create desire first, then offer the demo/sample as the response.

Use the demonstration principle the sample represents. Hopkins sold about 1 in 10 women when merely talking about his mother's silver polish, but nearly all when he could get inside the house and demonstrate it — 'a good product is its own best salesman.'
For ecommerce, replicate the demonstration with sampling programs, money-back guarantees, or in-home trials that require an explicit claim, then let the product do the selling.
caveats: Hopkins calls promiscuous sampling a 'very bad plan' from his direct-selling era; the transferable rule is that perceived value depends on an effort threshold, not on refusing all free sampling.
Gating raises friction — measure both claim rate and downstream conversion/repeat purchase rather than assuming fewer, better leads pay off.

cards.title: Give your brand a human personality
cards.summary: People love people more than corporations; giving your product or brand a named, personal spokesperson makes the creation famous along with the person.
cards.use_when: Building brand identity, creator-led content, founder-led marketing, or repositioning a faceless ecommerce brand in categories where competitors are all 'soulless corporations.'
steps: Decide whether the founder, a named expert, or a recurring persona will front the brand. Hopkins used a persona called Professor Anderson with an actual person behind it and said he did this wherever possible.

Make the person the face and voice of the advertising — not a stock model or a logo — because 'personalities appeal while soulless corporations do not. Make a man famous, and you make his creation famous.'

Have the person talk about the product's accomplishments and its making, since 'all of us love to study men and their accomplishments.' For ecommerce, this can be founder storytelling on the PDP, creator-style ad creative, or an expert answering objections on video.
Keep the persona consistent across channels so the human becomes a recognizable asset, consistent with the 'stick to what works' rule for campaigns.
Apply it especially where the founder is uniquely qualified: the person who built the product knows every in and out and is the best advocate for why customers should buy.
caveats: The Professor Anderson example is historical; the transferable claim is that personality aids persuasion, not that every brand needs a fictional persona.
Invented authority personas can breach modern ad-platform policies and consumer trust if they misrepresent expertise — prefer a real named person.

cards.title: Test, never assume your own taste predicts demand
cards.summary: Hopkins warns that judging products by personal preference has cost the advertising industry fortunes — the successes he doubted sold like crazy, so submit everything to the court of public opinion through testing.
cards.use_when: Deciding what products, creatives, or angles to launch or kill when you have a personal gut reaction for or against them.
steps: Separate your taste from the market's. Hopkins: 'We must never judge humanity by ourselves. The things we want, the things we like may appeal to a small minority.'
He explicitly says product selection goes wrong when operators reject products as 'stupid' that then sell hugely because the audience is billions of people, not the operator.

Write down your prediction before launching, then compare against actual performance — the practice mirrors Hopkins making mistakes in a small way and learning from each (he says he made no mistake twice).
Run small, cheap tests first rather than betting the campaign on a personal conviction, so the market rather than the operator adjudicates.
Record what worked and re-use it; Hopkins links this habit to developing enduring advertising principles, in contrast to repeatedly changing your mind based on your own impression of the creative.
caveats: Hopkins's argument is specifically against relying on personal preference and for empirical testing; it is not a formula for how many tests or what sample size to run.
Testing does not mean ignoring strategy or brand constraints — it means the audience, not the founder, is the judge of appeal.

cards.title: Stay close to the buyer and the money
cards.summary: Hopkins advises studying actual sellers (including canvassers and door-to-door salesmen) to learn what appeals work, and positioning your work near revenue-generating activity so you can capture a share of the value created.
cards.use_when: Doing customer research for ad angles, or negotiating roles, contracts, or agency compensation tied to advertising and sales performance.
steps: Study real sellers up close. Hopkins spent hours under torchlight listening to pitchmen and canvassers and said: 'Study salesmen, canvassers, and fakers if you want to know how to sell goods.' For ecommerce, this means watching sales calls, reading support tickets and chat logs, and interviewing repeat buyers — not just reading dashboards.
Watch for reactions, not just stated preferences: when you're close to the buyer, 'you can hear, you can see what they reject, you can see what appeal lights up their eyes.'
Document the specific phrases and objections that recur and test them as ad angles, since direct-response salespeople are the closest real-world laboratory for appeals that work.

On compensation, apply Hopkins's 'stay close to the money' principle: he moved from the expense side of a business to the sales-generating side, then negotiated a share of the sales he brought in (e.g., asking for a portion of the million dollars in toothpaste sales he generated).
Evidence value created and ask for a share of measured incremental value rather than flat fees disconnected from results.
caveats: 'Stay close to the money' is a career/business principle from Hopkins's autobiography, not a prescribed commission structure; deal terms vary by role and market.
'Fakers' in Hopkins's era includes deceptive pitchmen — study the mechanics of persuasion, not tactics that mislead buyers.

cards.title: Stick with the ad that works (moving parade)
cards.summary: You notice your own ads far more than customers do; Hopkins warns against changing successful campaigns out of boredom and says the best way to win new customers is usually the way that won millions.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to refresh or replace a profitable creative, offer, or PDP hero because it 'feels stale' internally.
steps: Before changing a working ad, distinguish internal boredom from market fatigue. 'The advertising becomes monotonous to the men who read every ad… they always come to want something new,' but customers have not read every ad.

Use the framing: you are not advertising to a standing army, you are advertising to a moving parade — most of your audience is seeing the message for the first time, which is why repetition across a changing audience keeps working.
Set a decision rule for refreshing: change when measured performance degrades, not on a fixed internal schedule or subjective creative boredom.
If you must change, keep the winning core (appeal, claim, offer) intact and swap the execution shell (imagery, format, channel), so you preserve what won millions and only vary the wrapper.
Record which principles have endured for you the way Hopkins kept his — this turns one-off wins into reusable rules rather than restarting from scratch each cycle.
caveats: This is Hopkins's stated preference for continuity, echoed later by David Ogilvy; some modern platforms show genuine creative fatigue, so treat 'never change' as the source's bias, not an absolute — reconcile with your own retention curves.
A moving parade still implies reach and frequency are being bought repeatedly; if you only ever reach the same small audience, repeated exposure can fatigue.

cards.title: Judge advertising by salesmanship and the customer's mind
cards.summary: Hopkins treats advertising as multiplied salesmanship whose success or failure is determined by whether the psychological appeal matches human nature — not by cleverness or personal taste.
cards.use_when: Choosing an appeal/angle before writing a campaign, or diagnosing why a campaign isn't converting despite decent execution.
steps: State the appeal in one sentence before writing: prevention, status/beauty, convenience, effort saved, time saved, etc. Hopkins says 'every advertising campaign depends on its psychology. Success or failure is determined by the right or wrong appeal.'

Check the appeal against what humans actually do: people 'do little to prevent' trouble but pursue rewards, happiness, beauty, and cheer — so test one dominant positive-outcome appeal before loading multiple appeals into one ad.
Apply the salesmanship standard to every executional question (length, tone, claims): 'Ask yourself, would this help a salesman sell the goods?' rather than following generic copywriting rules.

Because advertising is 'multiplied salesmanship,' the same mediocre message reaches your whole audience, so errors cost more than in person — raise the bar on the main promise before polishing anything else.

Use customer perspective as the final filter: no manufacturer should conduct his own advertising because he is too close to the factory and tells what he takes pride in rather than what the customer wants to know.
caveats: The 'right or wrong appeal' is a directional principle, not a guarantee; categories and audiences differ, and regulated categories constrain appeal choices.
Hopkins's own framework favors positive-outcome appeals; some products genuinely sell on risk-avoidance (insurance, security), so treat it as a starting hypothesis to test, not law.

cards.title: Prove the product, don't just talk about it
cards.summary: A dramatic demonstration converts far better than any argument; Hopkins sold roughly one in ten women by talk but nearly all by demonstration, and carried that principle into every campaign.
cards.use_when: Designing acquisition creative, PDP media, or landing page proof sections that currently rely on claims instead of showing the product working.
steps: Identify what a live demonstration would look like: the silver-polish example is the literal product applied to the buyer's own problem in front of them. For ecommerce, this means demo video, before/after, side-by-side, or a trial the customer physically experiences.
Prefer showing to arguing. Hopkins: 'No argument in the world can ever compare with one dramatic demonstration.' Replace persuasive copy with a visual proof asset where possible.
Get the product into the buyer's hands when feasible, since 'a good product is its own best salesman.' This is the rationale behind trials, guarantees, and in-home tests.
Choose demo formats that face the particular objection the buyer has — show cleaning power, fit, durability, or result timeline — rather than a generic brand film.
Keep demo creative central on the PDP and in paid ads, not buried; if the product genuinely wins on demonstration, make it the lead, not a supporting detail.
caveats: The one-in-ten versus 'nearly all' figures are Hopkins's door-to-door experience, not an ecommerce benchmark.
Demos must be accurate to real product performance; an exaggerated demo creates post-purchase returns and review damage.

cards.title: Capitalizing on insights: put your money where your copy is
cards.summary: Hopkins bought shares in the brand whose sales his advertising would lift, capturing the value he helped create — a model for tying compensation or investment to measurable performance you drive.
cards.use_when: Structuring performance-based deals, agency compensation, affiliate arrangements, or deciding how to bet on a product angle you believe will outperform.
steps: Apply the principle that 'the big salaries are paid to the salesmen... and to the men in the factory who reduce costs,' i.e., value accrues near revenue and profit creation — position your work and compensation close to that lever.
If you believe your creative will materially lift a brand's sales, negotiate a share of measured incremental value or performance-based terms rather than purely time-based fees.

Hopkins's Pepso dent example: he bought shares for $13,000 at the start of the project; the position paid him $200,000 in dividends and later sold for $500,000. Use this as an illustration of aligning upside with the results of your own work, not a promised return.
Build measurement into the deal up front — agree on what constitutes incremental sales attributable to advertising before the campaign begins.
For an operator running their own store, the analogous move is to reinvest in the channels and product angles with proven incremental lift instead of spreading budget evenly.
caveats: The Pepso dent numbers are a historical case study, not a benchmark; many campaigns don't produce that outcome and share-of-upside deals require trusted attribution.
Tying compensation to performance only works when sales lift can be reliably attributed — otherwise you are negotiating over an unmeasurable number.

cards.title: Do the work in volume with focus
cards.summary: Hopkins attributes his success to exceptional hours and volume of practice, not exceptional ability: working two or three times as much produces two or three times the mistakes and successes, and you learn from both.
cards.use_when: Building a sustainable creative testing cadence or deciding how much output an in-house or agency ecommerce marketing function should produce.
steps: Increase the volume of finished work — ads written, creatives shipped, tests run — rather than endlessly perfecting one asset, because volume is what generates both mistakes and successes to learn from.
Treat mistakes as the tuition: Hopkins says he learned from each and 'made no mistake twice,' turning errors into an operating record of enduring principles.
Pair volume with a learning log so insights from tests persist beyond the individual campaign and inform the next one.

Hopkins worked nights and Sundays (rarely an evening free for 16 years) and calls business a game he plays; the transferable mechanic is sustained focused repetitions in one domain, not the literal hours and not a recommendation to burn out.

Direct the volume at one thing you can go deep in — Hopkins says those with singular focus derive insights others simply won't have; for ecommerce, pick the domain (e.g., landing pages or paid creative) and do many deliberate reps.
caveats: Hopkins himself writes 'I am not advising others to follow my example' on the extreme hours; treat the durable lesson as focused volume, not the workaholism.
Volume without measurement or learning produces churn, not improvement — you still need to record what worked.

cards.title: Reframe advertising questions around the buyer's desires
cards.summary: Almost every ad question can be answered by asking what a good salesman would say if the individual prospect stood before him — starting with the prospect's expressed desires, not your product facts.
cards.use_when: Resolving copy, offer, or page-layout debates inside a team where opinions conflict and no test data yet exists.
steps: Identify the prospect's expressed desire first: for the sewing machine inquirer it was a sewing machine; for your store it may be a specific use case, budget, or occasion. 'Consider the person who stands before you with certain expressed desires.'
Answer the ad question in that person's terms: 'However big your business, get down to the units, for those units are all that make size.'

Cut lines that serve the brand's interests instead of the prospect's. Hopkins says 'argue anything for your own advantage and people will resist to the limit... seem unselfishly to consider your customer's desires and they will naturally flock to you.'

Test the creative against the standard 'Say only what you think a good salesman should say if that prospect stood before him' — this resolves disputes without waiting for an A/B test when budget or traffic is limited.
Use this as a fast internal filter before running the more expensive statistical test on the remaining, genuinely ambiguous options.
caveats: This is a judgment framework, not a substitute for measurement; where traffic allows, still validate against conversion data.
What the prospect 'wants to know' is inferred, not given — validate assumptions with support tickets, reviews, and sales conversations.

cards.title: Don't let success in one area convince you you can run any
cards.summary: Hopkins observes men make money in one business and lose it in others because success breeds the belief that they are super-businessmen — past success is not transferable competence.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to expand your store into an unrelated product category, new market, or a different business, especially when an existing product line is performing well.
steps: Inventory the specific competencies your current success depends on — sourcing, creative, fulfilment, audience — and ask which of these actually transfer to the proposed expansion.

Treat the planned move as a new business, not an extension of a proven one: Hopkins says 'it is curious how we all desire to excel in something outside of our own province. This leads many men astray.'
If expanding categories or markets, allocate a small test budget and staff it with people who do have domain experience, rather than assuming the core team's proven playbook carries over.
Watch for the moment confidence substitutes for evidence — the pattern Hopkins names is that one success makes people feel qualified to run anything.
Keep the proven core investment protected while the new venture is unproven, since losses in the new area can drain cash generated by the successful one.
caveats: This is a cautionary pattern, not a rule against diversification; adjacent expansions that share competencies may transfer well.
The claim is Hopkins's observation about businesses of his era; modern operators should still evaluate with their own data.

cards.title: Earn the role by demonstrating the work, not just applying
cards.summary: When Hopkins wanted a senior advertising job at a company with one of the largest budgets, he had dozens of people write testimonials, ran a daily newspaper column sharing his learning, and applied alongside the evidence — and won the role.
cards.use_when: Pitching a major retailer partnership, applying for an in-house leadership role, or winning a large client when you have no direct relationship and the competition is strong.
steps: Prepare proof of skill from third parties: Hopkins had dozens of people send letters vouching for his copywriting ability — for ecommerce, gather retailer logos, GMV case studies, or client statements.

Create a public body of work that the decision-maker will encounter: Hopkins wrote a daily newspaper column on advertising sharing everything he learned, so the hiring decision-maker saw his expertise repeatedly.
Do all the standard moves too — apply, call, try to meet — but treat those as the baseline, not the winning move, since the testimonials and column are what differentiated him.

Aim the pitch at the decision-maker's actual need, echoing Lasker's recruiting speech: acknowledge the best available copy still isn't good enough, then ask for exactly what's needed (e.g., 'give me three ads that will start the campaign').

Make the ask concrete and tied to a result, as Lasker did when offering any car on the street charged to him in exchange for three campaign-starting ads — pair a clear deliverable with a clear reward.
caveats: The job win is an anecdote from Hopkins's career, not a hiring guaranteed by this method.
The newspaper-column tactic relied on local print reach; adapt the 'public proof of work' to channels your target buyer actually sees.

playbook carries over.", "Watch for the moment confidence substitutes for evidence — the pattern Hopkins names is that one success makes people feel qualified to run anything.", "Keep the proven core
